To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

bilateral lesions of the dentate-interposed nucleus disrupt the conditioned eyelid response, but not startle or unconditioned eyelid responses, in the rat, a species in which eyelid conditioning has not been studied previously.
bilateral lesions in the dentate nucleus of the rat cerebellar nuclei disrupt eyelid conditioning.
bilateral lesions in the dentate-nucleus region of the rat cerebellar nuclei disrupt conditioned eyelid CRs, while leaving startle and unconditioned eyelid responses intact.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the cerebellum in classical conditioning.
the anatomical basis for the learning of a classically conditioned eyelid response in the rabbit.
the neural mechanisms of associative learning.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cerebellar system is necessary but not sufficient for eyelid conditioning in rabbits and rats.
the cerebellum is a critical structure for the acquisition and/or storage of the eyelid CR in the rabbit and in the rat.
cerebellar lesions produce deficits in conditioned eyelid responses, and this is true for both the rabbit and the rat.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cerebellum is necessary for the formation of CRs, but not URs.
the dentate-interpositional region of the cerebel-lar nuclei plays a critical role in the acquisition of eyelid conditioned responses.
the cerebellar cortex and the interpositus nucleus play a role in the learning of eyelid conditioning, but that other structures, such as the inferior olive, may also play a role in this learning.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cerebellum is a necessary component in the acquisition of a conditioned response.
the cerebellum has a critical role in the formation of eyelid conditioned responses.
we can condition the eyelid response in unrestrained rats, which opens up a whole range of possibilities for studying the cerebellar basis of eyelid CRs.
